ideas.title: Schema Storyteller
ideas.summary: Paste any database schema and get a plain-English narrative of what the data model means, who the actors are, and what constraints or indexes might be missing.
ideas.description: Developers onboarding to a new codebase spend hours reverse-engineering what a database schema actually represents in business terms. Schema Storyteller is a React + Vite single-page app where you paste SQL DDL, a Prisma schema, or a JSON Schema and Claude returns a readable entity-relationship narrative, business-domain vocabulary suggestions for cryptically named tables or columns, and a natural-language list of potentially missing constraints, indexes, or foreign keys. No backend required — the Claude API call runs client-side. The output can be exported as a Markdown file to drop into team documentation.
keyFeatures: Accepts SQL DDL, Prisma schema, and JSON Schema formats via paste or drag-and-drop
Generates plain-English entity descriptions and relationship narratives
Flags missing indexes, constraints, and nullable fields with natural-language explanations
One-click Markdown export for team documentation or onboarding wikis
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Claude API (client-side, no backend), file drag-and-drop
ideas.whyInteresting: Every developer has stared at a schema trying to figure out what 'tbl_ref_xmapping' actually means. This turns the reverse-engineering that currently lives in developers' heads into a shareable artifact, and it is buildable in an afternoon with a clear pedagogical and practical payoff.
ideas.inspiredBy: GitHub trending DevToys pattern (developer utility consolidation), HN Ask: What developer tool do you wish existed in 2026?

ideas.title: Concept Coverage Lens
ideas.summary: Upload a set of student code submissions for any programming assignment and get a per-student concept heatmap showing which CS concepts were demonstrated versus which were expected.
ideas.description: Instructors reviewing 30-60 student submissions rarely have time to notice whether a student solved a recursion problem with an imperative loop or bypassed a required data structure entirely. Concept Coverage Lens is a Flask + React dashboard where the instructor specifies the expected concepts for an assignment (e.g., recursion, linked list traversal, Big-O awareness) and uploads a batch of student code files. Claude analyzes each submission, maps the demonstrated CS concepts to a rubric, and generates a per-student heatmap alongside a class-wide gap report. An optional Canvas API integration lets instructors pull submissions without manual downloading. The report is exportable as a CSV for gradebook use.
keyFeatures: Instructor specifies expected concepts; Claude maps each submission against them
Per-student concept heatmap highlights missing or underdeveloped skills
Class-wide gap report shows which concepts most students bypassed or misapplied
Optional Canvas API integration for automated batch submission retrieval
ideas.techStack: Flask, React + Vite + Tailwind, Claude API, Canvas LMS API (optional), Supabase for session storage
ideas.whyInteresting: Automated graders tell instructors whether code passes tests, not whether students understood the underlying concept. This fills that gap and is directly useful for CS1/CS2 and DS&A courses where instructors suspect students are solving problems with the wrong conceptual tools.
ideas.inspiredBy: Need for scalable formative insight in large CS courses; Pisan's Jolly Feedback work revealing gaps between test-pass and conceptual understanding

ideas.title: Multi-Persona Code Review Simulator
ideas.summary: Students submit code to a panel of AI reviewers with distinct personas — Security Hawk, Performance Optimizer, Style Purist, and Grumpy Senior — then must respond to each review and iterate, building code-review soft skills alongside technical ones.
ideas.description: Real-world code review is as much a communication skill as a technical one, but most CS courses lack structured practice. Students build and submit a feature or module; Claude plays four reviewer personas with distinct foci and communication styles: the Security Hawk identifies injection and boundary risks, the Performance Optimizer flags O(n^2) loops and memory waste, the Style Purist enforces readability conventions, and the Grumpy Senior challenges design decisions with short skeptical comments. Each student must respond in writing — defending a choice or committing to a fix — before re-submitting. The platform tracks response quality over multiple iterations. The classroom assignment can be the platform itself (students build it) or the content inside it (students use it as a grading stage). Built with React + Supabase + Claude API.
keyFeatures: Four fixed reviewer personas with distinct focus areas and communication styles
Students must respond to each review comment (defend or commit to fix) before re-submitting
Diff view between submission versions to track what changed and whether review concerns were addressed
Instructor dashboard showing response quality patterns across the class
Configurable persona prompts so instructors can add domain-specific reviewers (e.g., Accessibility Auditor)
ideas.techStack: React + Vite + Tailwind, Supabase (auth + storage + real-time), Claude API, Monaco Editor for code display
ideas.whyInteresting: Code review is a top-cited skill gap in new-grad developers, yet it is almost never practiced in structured academic settings. This simulator gives students safe repetitions of an inherently adversarial but collegial process, and it scales without a TA per student.
ideas.inspiredBy: HN Show: Juggler (open-source GUI coding agent), industry surveys on new-grad soft-skill deficits in code review

ideas.title: Socratic Tutoring at the Proof-Concept Boundary: Extending and Evaluating LLM-Based CS Theory Tutoring for Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis
ideas.summary: The CHIRON system showed LLMs are only marginally viable as CS theory tutors, especially on proof-based questions. This research extends that evaluation framework to data structures and algorithm analysis, adds a symbolic consistency checker for complexity claims, and compares Socratic vs. direct-answer tutoring modes on learning outcomes.
ideas.description: CHIRON (SIGCSE TS 2026) evaluated GPT-4 as a tutor for automata theory, computability, and complexity using a five-criterion rubric, finding strong performance on conceptual explanation but systematic failure on proof-based questions such as reductions. Data structures and algorithm analysis (DS&A) courses present an analogous landscape: LLMs explain sorting algorithms fluently but generate incorrect Big-O complexity analyses, flawed loop-invariant proofs, and inconsistent recurrence derivations. This research (1) replicates and extends the CHIRON rubric to 18-20 DS&A subtopics using a question bank matched to Pisan's CSS 342/343 curriculum, (2) adds a symbolic consistency-checking layer — inspired by Pisan's functional-roles-of-equations work — that validates LLM-generated complexity claims against ground-truth recurrences before delivery to the student, and (3) runs a within-subjects comparison of Socratic mode vs. direct-answer mode on student engagement and error correction in a short DS&A lab. The result is both an empirical benchmark for LLM DS&A tutoring and a prototype correction mechanism grounded in symbolic reasoning, extending the composed-AI-tutor agenda Pisan has pursued across his career.

papers.title: Viability of Large Language Models as CS Theory Tutors
papers.authors: Three authors; United States Military Academy (West Point)
papers.abstract: CHIRON is an LLM-based tutoring system that uses Socratic interaction rather than direct answers to maximize student learning. The authors evaluated GPT-4 across 18 Theory of Computing subtopics (regular languages, context-free languages, Turing machines, decidability), using 10 average-student questions per subtopic scored on accuracy, completeness, clarity, pedagogical scaffolding, and follow-up quality. Overall results showed only marginal viability, with LLMs excelling at conceptual explanation but failing systematically on proof-based categories such as reductions.
papers.relevance: CHIRON establishes a replicable evaluation rubric and benchmark for LLM CS theory tutoring and directly identifies proof-based reasoning as the unresolved failure mode — the exact gap this research extends to DS&A courses where loop invariants, recurrences, and complexity proofs present the same challenge.

additionalRefs.title: Discerning Minds or Generic Tutors? Evaluating Instructional Guidance Capabilities in Socratic LLMs
additionalRefs.relevance: Provides a rigorous evaluation taxonomy for Socratic LLM tutoring capabilities across multiple dimensions, supplying complementary metrics beyond CHIRON's five-criterion rubric and situating the DS&A extension within the current state of the art on pedagogical assessment of AI tutors.

additionalRefs.title: The Promise and Limits of LLMs in Constructing Proofs and Hints for Logic Problems in Intelligent Tutoring Systems
additionalRefs.relevance: Directly characterizes where LLMs succeed and fail when generating step-by-step hints for proof-structured problems in ITSs, providing both motivating evidence for the symbolic consistency-checker component and a methodological prior for evaluating hint quality in structured symbolic domains.

additionalRefs.title: LeanTutor: Towards a Verified AI Mathematical Proof Tutor
additionalRefs.relevance: Demonstrates one architectural approach to combining LLM conversational fluency with automated verification (Lean theorem prover) for proof tutoring — a proof of concept for the symbolic-checker design this research adapts to algorithm complexity claims, where verified recurrences and Big-O bounds replace formal proofs.

additionalRefs.title: PEARL: Training Socratic Tutors with Pedagogically Aligned Reinforcement Learning
additionalRefs.relevance: Provides a principled training and evaluation framework for Socratic tutoring agents, offering both a comparison system against which the CHIRON-extended DS&A tutor can be benchmarked and a methodology for assessing whether the Socratic mode outperforms direct-answer delivery on learning outcomes.

researchPlan.overview: This six-month program replicates and extends the CHIRON evaluation framework from CS theory to data structures and algorithm analysis, adds a symbolic consistency checker for LLM-generated complexity claims, and tests whether Socratic vs. direct-answer mode affects student error correction in a real CSS 342 lab setting. The arc moves from benchmark construction to prototype development to controlled in-course evaluation, targeting SIGCSE or ICER for submission.

milestones.goal: Replicate CHIRON rubric, map CSS 342/343 syllabus to 18-20 DS&A subtopics, and build a 10-question-per-subtopic question bank covering sorting, trees, graphs, recurrences, loop invariants, and Big-O proofs
milestones.deliverable: Annotated question bank (180-200 questions) + rubric adaptation document mapping CHIRON criteria to DS&A context

milestones.goal: Run baseline LLM evaluation: query Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-4o with each question in both Socratic and direct modes; three raters score all responses using the extended rubric
milestones.deliverable: Scored evaluation dataset with inter-rater reliability report; identified top-failure subtopics (expected: recurrences, loop invariants)

milestones.goal: Design and implement the symbolic consistency checker: a module that parses LLM complexity claims (Big-O expressions, Master Theorem categorization, recurrence solutions) and validates them against a ground-truth lookup table or CAS (SymPy); flag inconsistent responses before delivery
milestones.deliverable: Working consistency-checker prototype; ablation study showing false-positive and false-negative rates on Month 2 dataset

milestones.goal: Re-evaluate the LLM+checker pipeline on the same question bank; measure claim-error reduction; identify remaining failure modes (narrative reasoning, induction-step errors) not caught by syntactic checking
milestones.deliverable: Comparative accuracy report (LLM alone vs. LLM+checker); revised failure taxonomy for DS&A tutoring

milestones.goal: Deploy a minimal tutoring interface in one CSS 342 lab session; students use Socratic mode for half the session and direct-answer mode for the other half on matched complexity problems; collect error-correction rates and brief exit surveys
milestones.deliverable: Pilot dataset (n~25-35 students); preliminary results on Socratic vs. direct mode effect on error identification

milestones.goal: Synthesize evaluation results, consistency-checker analysis, and pilot data; write and submit paper
milestones.deliverable: Submitted paper draft for SIGCSE TS 2027 or ICER 2027

researchPlan.resources: Access to CSS 342/343 course for question-bank alignment and one lab-session pilot (minimal disruption); Claude API and OpenAI API credits for evaluation runs; SymPy or Wolfram Alpha API for the complexity consistency checker; two student research assistants for rubric scoring and inter-rater reliability; existing Jolly Feedback submission logs for supplementary misconception context if needed.

risks.risk: LLM APIs improve rapidly, making a static evaluation snapshot feel stale by submission time
risks.mitigation: Design the question bank and rubric as a reusable benchmark artifact (publish alongside the paper); re-run evaluation on latest model at Month 4 to include a two-model comparison, which is itself a contribution

risks.risk: The symbolic consistency checker has high false-positive rates, incorrectly flagging valid complexity claims
risks.mitigation: Start with only unambiguous claim types (Master Theorem case assignments, polynomial Big-O comparisons) and report precision/recall explicitly; scope the checker narrowly so it adds value even if coverage is incomplete

risks.risk: One lab session is too short to observe statistically meaningful differences between Socratic and direct modes
risks.mitigation: Frame the pilot as a feasibility and direction-finding study (not a causal claim); use the session to calibrate effect size for a powered follow-up, which is itself reportable as a research contribution
